newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Kabul may fall to Taleban, top U.N. official says.
newsitem.headline: Kabul may fall to Taleban, top U.N. official says.

text.p: The Afghan Taleban militia may be on the verge of taking the country's capital of Kabul as government resistance to their onslaught seems to be crumbling, a top U.N. official said on Wednesday.

Under-Secretary General Marrack Goulding told reporters in New York the U.N. Security Council would meet later in the day to discuss the crisis in Afghanistan, but he held out little hope of a ceasefire or negotiations.
The advances by the radical Islamic Taleban threaten the survival of President Burhanuddin Rabbani's government.

"It is possible that Kabul is going to fall," said Goulding, who is in touch with U.N. officials in Kabul. He visited the country last week to try to broker negotiations that would end the long-running conflict.
"We are getting indications ... that Kabul may be on the point of falling," he added.

Goulding said he hoped the U.N. Security Council would endorse an appeal for a ceasefire and negotiations. But he said the Taleban militia showed little willingness to negotiate and there had been signs that government troops were defecting or refusing to fight in the face of the Taleban attacks, both in Kabul and earlier in other cities.
"If the Taleban think they achieve their objectives by military means, it's going to be very difficult to persuade them to get into negotiations," he said.

The Afghan government requested the U.N. Security Council meeting, saying in a letter that forces from neighbouring Pakistan had been involved in supporting the Islamist Taleban. The letter said it wanted the Security Council to respond to the "aggravated and alarming" situation.

The Taleban controls more than half of the central Asian country, which has been the scene of continual fighting between various Moslem and ethnic groups since Soviet troops supporting a communist government withdrew in 1989.

The Taleban, who emerged from the obscurity of religious schools in Pakistan two years ago, have been fighting to oust Rabbani and impose a strict Islamic order across Afghanistan. The Afghan government has often accused Pakistan of supporting the Taleban but Islamabad denies the charge.

The Islamic rebels thrust rapidly up the main highway to the capital through the precipitous Kabul river gorge after seizing the key town of Sarobi 44 miles (75 km) from Kabul during the night. They made spectacular gains in eastern Afghanistan this month.
